profile.summary: Habakkuk is a prophetic dialogue about perplexity in the face of violence, corruption and the apparent silence of God. The prophet exposes his distress because Judah is immersed in injustice, and God responds not with easy explanations, but with a vision of his sovereignty and holiness. The book shows that the Lord continues in control of history, will judge both the sin of Judah and that of the Babylonians, and calls the righteous to live by faith, trusting in the final righteousness of God.
profile.setting: The setting is Judah in the final period of its existence as an independent kingdom, amid the weakening of Assyria and the rise of Babylon in the late 7th century BC. Jewish society is marked by violence, idolatry and moral decay since the long period of previous wickedness, with brief reforms without lasting outcome. The exact date of the book is uncertain; the most common proposals place it between the end of Manasseh's reign and the first Babylonian invasion, with opinions that place him in the days of Manasseh, at the beginning of Josiah or in the time of Jehoiakim. The authorship is traditionally attributed to the prophet Habakkuk, of whom little is known beyond his ministry in Judah; an ancient tradition considers him Levite, but this is not certain.

structure.label: Complaint of Habakkuk and first divine response
structure.description: Habakkuk laments violence and injustice in Judah and questions why God does not seem to act. The Lord answers that he will raise up the Babylonians as an instrument of judgment against Judah.

structure.label: New perplexity and announcement of judgment on oppression
structure.description: The strange prophet further use of a more perverse people to punish Judah. God reaffirms that he will also judge the Babylonians and pronounce denunciations against corruption, oppression and false confidence in power.

structure.label: Prayer, memory of redemption and confession of trust
structure.description: Habakkuk pleads with mercy, poetically recalls God's redemptive action in the past and ends with a declaration of faith, joy in the Lord and trust despite circumstances.

themes: The sovereignty of God over history
The problem of evil and injustice
Trust and joy in the midst of the crisis
readingKeys: Note that the book does not offer a simple solution to evil, but a response centered on the character of God.
Realize the movement of dialogue: complaint, response, perplexity, new response and, finally, trust and praise.
Read chapter 3 as prayer and song of memory: it connects the difficult present to God's saving action in the past.
profile.cautions: The authorship and date of the book are not accurately known; historical reconstructions are probable, not absolute. The book does not promise complete explanations of suffering, but invites the reader to trust in the holy, just and sovereign God even when his actions seem time-consuming or incomprehensible.

dossier.narratedEra: The historical setting narrated in Habakkuk belongs to the end of the independent period of Judah, when internal violence was already striking and the Babylonian threat approached. The notes place the prophet amid the decline of Assyria, the rise of the Neo-Babyo-Babableonian Empire, and the final collapse of Judah. The book reflects this scenario of national crisis, with social injustice, judicial corruption and fear of foreign invasion.
dossier.compositionEra: The date of composition is presented as uncertain, but probably in the interval between about 645 BC and 605 BC, that is, in the final period of the monarchy of Judah before Babylonian exile. The notes record specific proposals: many put the book in the reign of Jehoiakim; they place it in the early years of Josiah; and the Jewish tradition mentioned associates it with the time of Manasseh. The traditional authorship is Habakkuk, a prophet of Judah; an ancient secondary proposal identifies him as a Levite, but this is only a hypothesis linked to a later textual tradition.

politics.title: Decline of the Assyrian Empire
politics.detail: The notes say that Habakkuk lived when Judah had long been under the power of Assyria, but the empire was weakening in the late 600s BC after previous military campaigns. The death of Asurbanípal and the loss of internal control paved the way for rebellions and the end of Assyrian hegemony.
politics.readingImpact: This helps to read prophecy in response to a real geopolitical transition: God is not speaking in abstract, but at a time when a dominant empire was ruined and another emerged to fulfill judgment.

politics.title: Rise of Babylon under Nabopolassar
politics.detail: The notes describe Nabopolassar (626-605 BC) proclaiming independence from Assyria and founding the Neo-babilonic Empire (626-539 BC). The fall of Nineveh in 612 BC, Haran in 609 BC and Carquemis in 605 BC are landmarks of the Babylonian advance.
politics.readingImpact: The reading of 1:5-11 gains historical weight: the "nation" that God would rise to discipline Judah is the power that was replacing Assyria in the regional domain.

politics.title: Nebuchadnezzar II and the aggression against Judah
politics.detail: The notes claim that under Nebuchadnezzar II (605-562 BC), Babylon campaigned against Judah and took Jerusalem on three occasions, culminating in the final destruction in 586 BC.
politics.readingImpact: This clarifies the logic of the judgment announcement: the book anticipates a real enemy that the original readers already knew or would come to know as an instrument of devastation.

politics.title: The inner instability of Judah from Manasseh to Josiah
politics.detail: The notes describe violence and injustice as traces of the society of Judah from the perverse reign of Manasseh, through Ammon, until the final years of Josiah, with reforms that did not produce lasting change. The internal political situation was therefore precarious, even under formally Davidic kings.
politics.readingImpact: This gives meaning to 1:2-4: the prophet's complaint is not generic; it is born of a Jewish society eroded by decades of infidelity, injustice and moral collapse.

politics.title: Debate on the exact reign of composition
politics.detail: The notes record three positions: Jehoshakim's time, the first years of Josiah, or Manasseh time. The introduction of Matthew Henry also favors Manasseh as a more likely conjecture, but recognizes uncertainty.
politics.readingImpact: The reader should treat any more specific date as a hypothesis, not as a closed data; the central message depends more on the pre-exile crisis scenario than of a precise year.

customs.title: Corrupted judicial life
customs.detail: The note of 1:4 says that injustice was visible even in the courts, where the law no longer worked to maintain justice.
customs.readingImpact: This shows that the problem denounced by Habakkuk was not only private but institutional moral; the prophecy confronts the bankruptcy of public order.

customs.title: Practice of sentinel and vigilant hope
customs.detail: In 2:1, the prophet describes himself as a watchman in a guard, awaiting the divine response.
customs.readingImpact: The image communicates attitude of obedient expectation: the prophet not only protests, but remains attentive to hear and adjust his understanding to God's response.

customs.title: Economy of estate, exile and prey
customs.detail: The notes feature the Babylonians as plunderers, oppressive collectors and conquerors who strip nations, take captives and build power through violence and fraud.
customs.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the book condemns concrete economic and military practices - plundering, extortion, unjust enrichment - and not just "mal" in an abstract sense.

customs.title: Construction of cities and houses by dishonest means
customs.detail: In 2:9-11 and 2:12-14, the notes speak of large houses and cities built with deceit, corruption, and bloodshed.
customs.readingImpact: This reinforces that God's judgment reaches social and urban structures, not only individuals; the prosperity built on injustice is presented as a final loss.

customs.title: Idolatric worship and comparison with the temple
customs.detail: The notes contrast the Babylonian idols, unable to save or teach, with the Lord enthroned in his holy temple. They also recall that in the time of Habakkuk, the temple of Jerusalem was the place of the divine presence on earth.
customs.readingImpact: The contrast guides devotional and theological reading: the center of the book is not imperial power, but the living God who rules history and demands exclusive worship.

customs.title: Memory of the Exodus as a resource of worship and hope
customs.detail: In chapter 3, the prophet prays and sings in the form of a psalm, recalling the redemption of the exodus. Reading emphasizes language of divine warfare, cosmic signs and crossing of the sea.
customs.readingImpact: The cultural and poetic context turns the lament into worship: the community is invited to remember that the God who judged Egypt can also act for Judah.

language.title: "Message/oracle." as prophetic opening
language.detail: In 1:1, the initial word is explained as "message" or "oracle," marking the book as a revelation of God through the prophet.
language.readingImpact: This frames the book as an authorized divine pronouncement, not as mere personal outburst.

language.title: Reason for clamor and response
language.detail: The 1:2 notes highlight the literary pattern of calling for help and not being heard immediately, and associate trust and communion with God.
language.readingImpact: The language of dialogue shows that biblical faith can include reverent lament; the book legitimizes questions before God.

language.title: Vocabulary of violence and predatory images
language.detail: In 1:8, the Babylonians are compared to fast and ferocious animals; in 1:14-15, the metaphor of fishermen with hooks, nets and fish depicts people caught by conquest.
language.readingImpact: These images make imperial cruelty concrete and vivid, helping the reader to feel the asymmetry between vulnerable Judah and the predatory aggressor.

language.title: "Fé/fidelity" at 2:4
language.detail: The note explains that the Hebrew word presented as faith/fidelity points to a way of life that trusts in God and reproduces its ethical standards.
language.readingImpact: The central phrase of the book is not only doctrinal; it redefines the just as one whose trust translates into practical loyalty.

language.title: The five inaccuracies/taunt songs
language.detail: In 2:6-20, the notes identify five songs of mockery or mockery, each with denunciation, judgment and reason of the judgment.
language.readingImpact: The literary structure shows that the chapter is not a random collection of oracles, but a poetic judicial process against violence and idolatry.

language.title: Theophanic Poem and the Divine Warrior Language
language.detail: Chapter 3 is described as a psalm-shaped prayer, with images of pestilence, plague, sea, rivers, sun and moon, as well as reminiscences of Sinai and the exodus.
language.readingImpact: Language extends reading: God is not passive in the face of history; he appears as a redeeming warrior who dominates creation and intervenes for his people.

timeline.title: End of Assyrian rule over Judah and crisis of the 7th century BC.
timeline.detail: The notes place Habacuk in the period when Assyria was still power, but already gave signs of collapse, with the composition probably in the late 7th century BC.
timeline.readingImpact: Prophecy should be read in response to an imperial world in recomposition, not as reflection outside of time.

timeline.title: Fall of Nineveh, Haran and Carchemis
timeline.detail: The approximate dates of 612, 609 and 605 BC are indicated as milestones of the Assyrian defeat to Babylon.
timeline.readingImpact: These events explain why the text speaks of a new aggressive power; the international scene is changing rapidly.

timeline.title: Last decades of Judah before exile
timeline.detail: The introduction states that the prophecy fits better between about 645 BC and 605 BC, before Babylonian exile.
timeline.readingImpact: This interval helps to realize the urgency of the warnings: the time for repentance was already running out.

timeline.title: 605-586 BC: Babylonian campaigns against Judah
timeline.detail: The notes mention that the Babylonians took captives of Judah between 605 and 586 BC, culminating in the final fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader understands 1:5-11 and 1:9 as an announcement of something that would become historically verifiable in the national experience of Judah.

timeline.title: According to Jewish tradition and the hypothesis of Manasseh
timeline.detail: Matthew Henry records the Jewish tradition and the chronological proposal that place Habakkuk in the reign of Manasseh, while the introduction of Tyndale mentions this same proposal as one of the three positions debated.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader should note that this chronology is traditional and debated, useful for placing the report of apostasy, but not definitive.

investigation: Tyndale's introduction is the main historical basis; it offers the most detailed political framework, but it also presents chronological uncertainties.

Matthew Henry adds ancient traditions and conjectures, especially about the person of Habakkuk and the possible relationship with Bel and the Dragon, but these traditions are not confirmed by the note itself and remain secondary.
Tyndale's notes favor literary and theological reading; therefore, some cultural data appear indirectly, especially in images of war, courts, commerce and worship.
There is no secure information on the prophet's family, domestic life, daily food from Judah or extensive social class details; any expansion on these topics would require additional sources.
References to Bel and the Dragon, to the Levitical identity and to the possible encounter with Daniel are mentioned only as tradition or conjecture, not as established facts.
The dates and reigns listed here are approximate and follow the tracks and names explained in the notes; no more accurate schedules were inferred than the sources authorize.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends solely on the annexed notes and therefore is selective: it covers more strongly the imperial backdrop, the internal crisis of Judah, the literary images and the theological structure of the book. There are real gaps in topics such as family, domestic routines, food, specific crafts and details of daily worship, because the sources do not develop them. There is also controversy about the exact date of composition and the most accurate identity of the prophet; therefore, these questions were marked as debated when appropriate. The material is consciously confessional and devotional in its tone, but here it was organized historically-culturally for Protestant evangelical reading, without extrapolating beyond what the notes claim.
